column1: # Survivors of ./tests/mutation/run-generated.sh -- mutants the suite did NOT kill.
# A real-gap gets a test written, and then a corpus entry so the new test is
# itself proved capable of failing. An equivalent mutant changes text without
# changing behaviour and can never be killed by anything - it is not a defect.
# Rows are keyed on (file, mutation); the line number is informational and may
# be stale. Only targets swept by the last run are rewritten.

column5: note

-e also accepts a non-directory, and that is the only state that separates the two: with a regular file at the lock path the real cgi queues a request and answers 'A scan will be started within one minute' while the mutant answers 'A scan is already in progress' and queues nothing; with a directory there both outputs are byte-identical (measured). The stack creates that path only with mkdir (scan.sh:20) and removes it only with rm -rf (its EXIT trap), so the divergent state is not one it can reach - the same class as the -f/-e rows already triaged wontfix in survivors.tsv. In that state the mutant is not the worse of the two either: the real code promises a scan that can never run, because scan.sh's own mkdir fails on the same non-directory and exits 75, so the poller defers that request forever.

Same class once more: only a non-directory at the marker separates them. Measured with a regular file at DUC_REQUEST_DIR - real: exit 0, no scan, the stray file left in place; mutant: a full index runs and the file is deleted by the rm -rf in the 0) arm. With a directory at that path both are identical. Nothing in the stack writes a non-directory there (the cgi mkdir -p's it, this file rm -rf's it), and in that state the mutant is doing the ordinary thing the protocol does with a marker rather than introducing a defect.

Every unguarded command in this file but one is the last command of its case arm, where aborting and falling through give the same exit status and the same side effects - measured on the 0) arm with a blocked rm -rf: rc=1 on both variants. The exception is the *) arm's rm -rf, which is followed by the 'Manual scan failed (exit N)' line: with the marker's parent unwritable and the scan failing 5, the real code exits 1 having logged nothing while the mutant logs the failure and exits 0. The state that would have to exist is a REQUEST_DIR the poller cannot remove while the log stays writable - the poller runs as root (the compose service sets no user:) and the marker is /tmp/scan_requested under a 1777 /tmp, so the container cannot reach it; and a test built on a chmod 0500 parent would silently stop being able to fail the moment the suite ran as root, which is the shape docs/TEST-HARDENING-LOG.md section 8 warns about. In the divergent state the mutant is also the better of the two: it records the failure the real code swallows.

column3: read -r -p "Remove it? [y/N] " -n 1 REPLY || true ==> read -r -p "Remove it? [y/N] " -n 1 REPLY && true
column5: the failing read is the non-final command of an AND-OR list, and errexit exempts exactly that position, so 'read ... && true' cannot fire -e any more than 'read ... || true' can; the list's own status (1 after EOF, 0 otherwise) is read by nothing, because the next statement is an echo and the branch test reads REPLY, which :78 pre-clears. Measured both variants over 16 combinations of stdin (EOF, y, Y, n, N, bare newline, an unrelated character, a leading space before y) x stdin_is_tty 0/1: byte-identical stdout, stderr and exit status, EOF included - that being the case the || true was written for. Mechanism demonstrated separately: bash -c 'set -e; false && true; echo continued' continues with the list status 1, while the assignment form at :52 - the row above - does exit, which is why two identical-looking operators get different verdicts here. The guard itself is not dead: deleting the || true outright would abort on Ctrl-D, since a bare failing read is not in an exempt position

Measured both variants over 486 scenarios - gluetun and sonarr each {tunnel IP, WAN IP, unreachable} x the four tunneled services each {match, other IP, unreachable} - byte-identical stdout, stderr and exit status throughout. The separating state is again a stdout that refuses every write: there the original stops at the first failed echo (one write error on stderr) while the mutant runs the whole report (ten), both exiting 1. In the context this actually runs in - cron, stdout is a pipe - a consumer that goes away closes the pipe instead of failing writes, and that case is identical: './check-vpn.sh | head -1' is killed by SIGPIPE at status 141 in both variants

errexit is not load-bearing for anything this script can fail: the docker inspect at :38 is an if-condition, the docker exec|grep|grep at :56-58 ends in `|| true`, and the tailscale set at :66 is an if-condition, so no failing command is left unguarded. Measured both variants over 120 scenarios - inspect {running, stopped, missing, empty} x prefs {bare 41641, quoted, wrong port, no credential in the file, docker exec fails} x tailscale set {0, 7} - and stdout, stderr and exit status are byte-identical in every one. The single state that separates them is a stdout that refuses every write (fd closed before exec, or ENOSPC): there the -e version dies at the first failed echo with status 1 where the mutant continues to its own exit 0. That state cannot arise from the systemd --user timer this runs under, whose stdout is the journal socket, and a test for it would be asserting bash's write-error semantics rather than anything this script promises
